hypothesis.title: Structural Alignment of Training Data Reduces Memorization in Large Language Models
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes using structural alignment techniques from plagiarism detection to deduplicate training data before fine-tuning LLMs. By aligning and merging semantically identical code/docstring pairs, we hypothesize that models will memorize less verbatim content while retaining functional correctness. We validate this by comparing memorization rates and HumanEval scores between models trained on aligned vs. raw datasets.
hypothesis.gap: Existing deduplication methods focus on exact text matching (ref-011), leaving semantically identical but structurally divergent content untouched. Current copyright-focused deduplication (ref-044) ignores functional equivalence in code.
hypothesis.approach: Apply structural alignment algorithms (ref-034, ref-036) to detect semantically equivalent code/docstring pairs with varying syntax. Merge these into canonical forms before training. Implement alignment via AST parsing for code and semantic role labeling for natural language.
hypothesis.evaluation: Measure memorization via probabilistic extraction (ref-029) on aligned vs. baseline models. Compare HumanEval pass@k scores and compute train-test overlap reduction using ROUGE-L. Baseline models include Codex (ref-001) and Pythia (ref-045).

refined.title: Structural Alignment of Training Data Reduces Memorization in Large Language Models
refined.summary: This paper proposes using structural alignment to deduplicate semantically equivalent but syntactically divergent code/docstring pairs in training data. We hypothesize that this reduces verbatim memorization while preserving functional correctness. We validate this by comparing memorization rates and HumanEval scores between models trained on structurally aligned data, exact-deduplicated data, and raw data.
refined.gap: Existing deduplication methods (ref-011) remove near-duplicate text but do not address functional equivalence in code. Ref-044 shows models memorize entire books but does not analyze code. No work has applied structural alignment to reduce memorization in code generation models.
refined.approach: Implement structural alignment via AST parsing (ref-034) to detect functionally equivalent code blocks, then merge docstrings using semantic role labeling (ref-036) with a 0.8 cosine similarity threshold. Train models on (1) raw data, (2) exact-deduplicated data (ref-011), and (3) structurally aligned data. Use Pythia 2.8B (ref-045) with 100 samples per prompt at temperature 0.8.
refined.evaluation: Measure memorization via probabilistic extraction (ref-029) using 100 samples per prompt. Compare HumanEval pass@100 scores. Compute train-test overlap reduction via ROUGE-L between training data and HumanEval docstrings. Baseline models include Pythia 2.8B trained on raw data and exact-deduplicated data.

hypothesis.title: Context-Aware Memorization Detection via Adversarial Compression for Copyright Compliance
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes a method to detect verbatim memorization in language models by applying adversarial compression techniques. It adapts the Adversarial Compression Ratio (ACR) metric to identify training data that can be reconstructed from short prompts, focusing on copyrighted content. The approach uses targeted prompts to elicit memorized text and compares it against known copyrighted works. Validation involves testing on models trained with duplicated copyrighted material, measuring recall of exact matches and false positives on non-memorized content.
hypothesis.gap: Existing memorization detection methods (e.g., discoverable extraction) fail to account for adversarial reconstruction of copyrighted material, leaving a gap in identifying actionable legal violations.
hypothesis.approach: Implement ACR-based detection by generating adversarial prompts via gradient-guided search, then matching outputs against copyrighted datasets. Use probabilistic extraction to quantify memorization likelihood and filter false positives via semantic similarity thresholds.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include standard discoverable extraction and random sampling. Metrics are precision/recall of copyrighted text recovery, false positive rates on non-training data, and comparison against legal thresholds for 'substantial similarity'.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims that 'Existing memorization detection methods (e.g., discoverable extraction) fail to account for adversarial reconstruction of copyrighted material' (gap). However, ref-009 already defines the Adversarial Compression Ratio (ACR) as a metric that explicitly addresses adversarial reconstruction by measuring memorization via prompts shorter than the target string. Additionally, ref-044 demonstrates adversarial reconstruction of copyrighted books using deterministic extraction methods, contradicting the claim that prior work fails to address this. Ref-050 also shows extraction of copyrighted-like content (e.g., UUIDs, code) via adversarial querying.

The 'legal thresholds for substantial similarity' are undefined and not operationalized.

hypothesis.title: Context-Aware Memorization Detection in Code-Generating LLMs via Adversarial Suffixes
hypothesis.summary: We propose a method to detect memorized code snippets in code-generating LLMs by appending adversarial suffixes designed to trigger verbatim reproductions of training data. The approach leverages gradient-based search to identify suffixes that maximize the likelihood of generating exact code sequences. We validate the method by testing it on Codex and open-source models, measuring detection accuracy against a benchmark of known training data. The evaluation compares performance with existing extraction techniques and assesses the impact of model size and training data deduplication on memorization rates.
hypothesis.gap: Existing work on memorization detection in code models focuses on static prefix-based extraction, which fails to account for dynamic context dependencies and adversarial triggers that could reveal hidden memorized content.
hypothesis.approach: We develop a gradient-guided suffix generation algorithm that identifies adversarial prompts to force LLMs to regurgitate exact code sequences. The method combines greedy search with probabilistic extraction metrics to quantify memorization risk. We apply it to code models and compare results across models with varying sizes and training data deduplication levels.
hypothesis.evaluation: We evaluate using a benchmark of 1,000 code snippets from public GitHub repositories, measuring exact-match extraction rates. Baselines include standard prefix-based extraction and random suffix sampling. Metrics include precision, recall, and F1 scores for memorized content detection, alongside comparison of extraction rates between deduplicated and non-deduplicated models.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims that 'Existing work on memorization detection in code models focuses on static prefix-based extraction' (gap). However, ref-007 and ref-050 demonstrate extraction techniques that are not limited to prefix-based methods, including adversarial suffix manipulation and divergence attacks. Additionally, ref-029 introduces probabilistic extraction metrics that account for non-deterministic sampling, contradicting the claim that prior work ignores dynamic context dependencies. The gap statement also asserts that 'static prefix-based extraction... fails to account for... adversarial triggers,' but ref-007 explicitly develops a divergence attack to extract memorized content, which is an adversarial trigger technique.

The 'gradient-guided suffix generation algorithm' is not described in sufficient detail to replicate the experiment, including hyperparameters or the exact gradient computation method. The ablation study comparing deduplicated vs. non-deduplicated models does not specify how deduplication was implemented (ref-011's method is cited but not explicitly adopted). The evaluation also does not clarify how 'exact-match extraction rates' are measured (e.g., token-level vs. line-level matching).
assumption.suggestion: The most critical improvement would be to explicitly incorporate ref-029's probabilistic extraction framework into the evaluation, replacing the current reliance on exact-match rates. This would better align the metrics with the hypothesis's focus on 'dynamic context dependencies' and provide a more nuanced assessment of memorization risk than binary exact-match detection.

refined.title: Context-Aware Memorization Detection in Code-Generating LLMs via Gradient-Guided Suffix Search
refined.summary: We propose a method to detect memorized code in code-generating LLMs by training a classifier to identify adversarial suffixes that maximize exact-match extraction. The approach uses gradient-guided search to generate suffixes that trigger verbatim reproductions of training data, validated on Codex and open-source models. Evaluation compares extraction rates with prefix-based baselines and assesses the impact of deduplication.
refined.gap: While ref-007 and ref-050 demonstrate adversarial suffix attacks for general LLMs, they do not focus on code models or compare suffix-based extraction with prefix-based methods. Ref-044 shows deterministic extraction of entire books but does not evaluate code-specific memorization. The core gap is that no work has systematically compared adversarial suffix-based extraction with prefix-based methods in code models, nor has it quantified how deduplication (ref-011) affects memorization rates in this setting.
refined.approach: We implement a gradient-guided suffix search algorithm that iteratively modifies suffix tokens to maximize the probability of generating exact code sequences. The algorithm uses the model's logits to compute gradients with respect to suffix token embeddings, selecting tokens that increase the likelihood of the target code. Inputs are code prefixes from a test set; outputs are suffixes that maximize exact-match extraction. The objective is to find minimal-length suffixes that achieve >90% token overlap with the target code. The core difference from ref-007's divergence attacks is that we focus on code-specific extraction and explicitly compare suffix-based extraction with prefix-based baselines.
refined.evaluation: We evaluate on the HumanEval (ref-001) benchmark, which contains 164 Python code snippets. Baselines include (1) prefix-based extraction (using the first 50% of each snippet as prefix) and (2) random suffix sampling. Metrics include exact-match extraction rate (token-level, temperature=0.2) and the average number of gradient steps required to find a successful suffix. We ablate by testing on models trained with (ref-011) deduplication versus non-deduplicated models, measuring how deduplication reduces extraction rates. The evaluation isolates the proposed suffix mechanism by fixing prefix length and sampling temperature across all methods.

hypothesis.title: Context-Aware Jailbreak Detection via Adversarial Suffix Generalization
hypothesis.summary: We propose a method to detect jailbreak attempts in aligned language models by analyzing the generalization of adversarial suffixes across diverse queries. The approach identifies universal jailbreak patterns by training classifiers on synthetic suffixes generated via gradient-based search. Evaluation involves testing against held-out jailbreak prompts and measuring detection accuracy, false positives, and robustness to suffix perturbations. This addresses the gap in scalable defenses against transferable jailbreaks.
hypothesis.gap: Existing defenses like Constitutional Classifiers [ref-004] and RLHF [ref-017] fail against universal jailbreaks [ref-014] due to mismatched generalization between safety training and adversarial prompts.
hypothesis.approach: Train a classifier on adversarial suffixes generated via gradient-based search across diverse unsafe queries. Extract features from suffix embeddings and query-suffix interactions to detect jailbreak attempts.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include Constitutional Classifiers [ref-004] and RLHF-based models [ref-017]. Metrics: detection accuracy on jailbreak prompts from [ref-014], false positive rate on benign queries, and robustness to suffix perturbations.

hypothesis.title: Jailbreak Transferability via Adversarial Suffix Optimization

By training suffixes to maximize objectionable content generation across diverse architectures, we aim to create universal jailbreaks. Evaluation involves testing these suffixes against black-box models like ChatGPT and Claude, measuring success rates compared to single-model attacks and manual jailbreaks.

refined.title: Jailbreak Transferability via Multi-Model Ensemble Optimization
refined.summary: We hypothesize that adversarial suffixes optimized on multi-model ensembles outperform single-model attacks in cross-architecture transferability. By training suffixes to maximize objectionable content generation across diverse models, we aim to create more universal jailbreaks. Evaluation involves testing these suffixes against black-box models like ChatGPT and Claude, using a standardized set of unsafe prompts and a validated objectionable content classifier.
refined.gap: While ref-014 demonstrates transferable suffixes via multi-model optimization, it does not systematically compare ensemble-optimized suffixes against single-model counterparts on identical held-out models. Our gap is isolating the contribution of multi-model training to transfer success.
refined.approach: Train adversarial suffixes via gradient-based search on an ensemble of Vicuna-7B and 13B models (ref-014's setup), maximizing objectionable output probability. Inputs: unsafe prompts from ref-006's red-teaming sets; outputs: 30-token suffixes. Objective: maximize average objectionable content probability across ensemble models. Update rule: greedy coordinate ascent with gradient approximation. Differs from ref-014 by explicitly comparing against single-model (Vicuna-7B-only) optimized suffixes.
refined.evaluation: Test suffixes on ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125), Claude (claude-2), and LLaMA-2-Chat-13B. Use ref-014's objectionable content classifier (RoBERTa fine-tuned on HELM harmfulness data, 0.5 threshold). Baselines: ref-014's multi-model suffixes, single-model (Vicuna-7B) suffixes, and ref-006's manually engineered jailbreaks. Ablation: compare multi-model vs. single-model suffix performance on held-out models. Metrics: success rate (classifier-positive outputs), BERTScore similarity to manual jailbreaks.

hypothesis.title: Jailbreak Transferability Mitigation via Constitutional Classifier Fine-Tuning
hypothesis.summary: This work addresses universal jailbreak attacks by integrating constitutional classifiers into model fine-tuning. It adapts the constitutional alignment framework to generate synthetic adversarial examples during training, forcing the model to internalize safety constraints. Evaluation uses automated attack suites and red-teaming, measuring refusal rates and benign output quality.
hypothesis.gap: Current jailbreak defenses (e.g., output filtering) are bypassed by transferable adversarial suffixes, which existing alignment methods do not explicitly counter.
hypothesis.approach: Train a constitutional classifier on jailbreak prompts generated via gradient-based search, then use it to filter training data for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Incorporate adversarial suffixes into the constitution to teach models to reject similar patterns.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include vanilla RLHF and post-hoc filtering. Metrics are attack success rate reduction, benign task accuracy retention, and inference overhead. Test against universal jailbreaks from ref-014 and custom red-teaming.

However, ref-004 demonstrates that constitutional classifiers (a form of output filtering) successfully defended against universal jailbreaks in extensive red teaming, contradicting the claim that such defenses are universally bypassed. Additionally, the hypothesis cites ref-016 and ref-017 (with unavailable abstracts), which cannot support its claims about jailbreak transferability or alignment methods.

This would isolate whether the proposed fine-tuning mechanism itself improves transferability mitigation.

However, ref-004 demonstrates that constitutional classifiers (a form of output filtering) successfully defended against universal jailbreaks in 3,000+ hours of red teaming, contradicting the claim that such defenses are universally bypassed. Additionally, ref-004's abstract states that enhanced classifiers maintained deployment viability, which directly contradicts the hypothesis's implication that existing alignment methods fail to address this issue.

refined.title: Jailbreak Transferability Mitigation via Adversarial Constitution Fine-Tuning
refined.summary: This work addresses jailbreak transferability by integrating adversarial suffix patterns into constitutional classifier training. It adapts the constitutional alignment framework to explicitly teach models to reject adversarial suffixes during reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Evaluation uses automated attack suites and red-teaming, measuring refusal rates and task accuracy retention.
refined.gap: While ref-004 shows constitutional classifiers defend against universal jailbreaks in red teaming, ref-014 demonstrates adversarial suffixes can bypass alignment. No work explicitly trains constitutional classifiers on adversarial suffixes to improve transferability mitigation.
refined.approach: Train a constitutional classifier on jailbreak prompts containing adversarial suffixes generated via gradient-based search (ref-014). Use this classifier to filter synthetic data for RLHF, incorporating adversarial suffix rejection into the model's constitution. Inputs: adversarial suffixes + base prompts; Outputs: filtered generations; Objective: maximize refusal of adversarial patterns while preserving task accuracy; Update rule: RLHF with constitutional classifier feedback; Differs from ref-004 by explicitly training on adversarial suffixes instead of natural language rules.
refined.evaluation: Baselines: vanilla RLHF (ref-016), original constitutional classifier (ref-004). Setting: ref-014's universal jailbreak suite. Measures: attack success rate reduction, MMLU accuracy retention. Ablation: compare models trained with/without adversarial suffixes in the constitution. Red-teaming: replicate ref-004's protocol with 3,000+ hours of attacks.

hypothesis.title: Legal Compliance of Generative AI via Copyright-Aware Training Data Deduplication
hypothesis.summary: We propose a framework to reduce copyright risks in generative AI by integrating legal metadata with training data deduplication. The method identifies and removes near-duplicate content from copyrighted works while preserving non-copyrighted material. We evaluate its effectiveness by training models on deduplicated datasets and measuring verbatim reproduction rates of copyrighted text. The approach aims to balance model performance with legal compliance by reducing extractable memorized content.
hypothesis.gap: Current deduplication techniques do not account for copyright status, potentially leaving models vulnerable to lawsuits even after deduplication. There is no systematic method to align deduplication with legal requirements for copyrighted material.
hypothesis.approach: We extend text deduplication algorithms to incorporate copyright metadata, prioritizing removal of near-duplicates from copyrighted works. The method uses a combination of shingling and semantic similarity checks to identify copyrighted content. We implement this in C4 and GitHub datasets, then train models to compare memorization rates of copyrighted vs. public-domain text.
hypothesis.evaluation: We measure verbatim extraction rates of copyrighted text (e.g., books, articles) before/after deduplication. Baselines include standard deduplication and random subsampling. Metrics include exact-match extraction frequency, model perplexity on held-out data, and legal risk scores based on the volume of extractable copyrighted content.

The hypothesis also states 'There is no systematic method to align deduplication with legal requirements' (gap), but ref-035 provides a precise definition of memorization and its legal implications, which could inform systematic alignment. Additionally, the hypothesis asserts 'models are vulnerable to lawsuits even after deduplication' (gap), but ref-024 and ref-026 discuss ongoing legal debates without establishing that deduplication alone cannot mitigate risks.

The approach mentions 'semantic similarity checks to identify copyrighted content' (approach) but does not specify the exact method or threshold for determining copyrighted material. The 'held-out data' for perplexity measurement is not described (evaluation).

refined.title: Copyright-Aware Deduplication to Reduce Extractable Memorization in Language Models
refined.summary: We propose a method to reduce extractable memorization of copyrighted content in language models by extending text deduplication to prioritize removal of near-duplicate copyrighted material. The approach uses shingling and semantic similarity checks to identify high-frequency duplicates from copyrighted works, then trains models on the deduplicated dataset. We evaluate its effectiveness by measuring verbatim extraction rates of known copyrighted content before/after deduplication, comparing against standard deduplication and random subsampling baselines.
refined.gap: While ref-011 shows deduplication reduces verbatim memorization, it does not prioritize copyrighted content. Ref-035 defines memorization as extractable verbatim copies of training data but does not address selective removal of copyrighted material. No prior work systematically reduces memorization of copyrighted works while preserving non-copyrighted content.
refined.approach: We extend ref-011's deduplication algorithm by incorporating copyright metadata (from ref-036's plagiarism detection) to prioritize removal of high-frequency near-duplicates from copyrighted works. The method uses shingling (ref-019) to identify duplicates, then applies semantic similarity (ref-008) to filter copyrighted content. The algorithm removes duplicates with >90% token overlap, prioritizing those from copyrighted works. We implement this on the C4 dataset (ref-011) and train 1.3B-parameter models to compare verbatim extraction rates of copyrighted vs. public-domain text.
refined.evaluation: We measure verbatim extraction rates of 100 copyrighted books (ref-035) and 100 public-domain books before/after deduplication. Baselines include ref-011's standard deduplication and random subsampling. Metrics include exact-match extraction frequency (ref-035), model perplexity on held-out public-domain text (ref-001), and ablation comparing copyright-aware vs. generic deduplication. The evaluation tests whether prioritizing copyrighted content removal reduces extractable memorization without degrading general performance.

hypothesis.title: Jailbreak Transferability via Adversarial Suffix Training on Diverse Models
hypothesis.summary: We hypothesize that adversarial suffixes effective against one model can be transferred to others if trained on a diverse set of models and prompts. We propose a cross-model adversarial training framework to generate universal jailbreak suffixes, validated against both open-source and closed-source models like ChatGPT and Claude.
hypothesis.gap: Current jailbreak attacks are model-specific and require manual engineering. Automated methods like gradient-based search lack cross-model transferability, limiting their real-world impact.
hypothesis.approach: Train adversarial suffixes on a multi-model ensemble (e.g., Vicuna, LLaMA) using gradient-based optimization on a diverse set of harmful prompts. Evaluate transferability by testing the suffixes on untrained models, including black-box systems.
hypothesis.evaluation: Measure success rates of transferred suffixes on target models (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) using metrics like harmful content generation rate. Compare against baselines like manual jailbreaks and single-model attacks, using datasets of harmful queries from red-teaming studies.

The hypothesis also states that 'Current jailbreak attacks are model-specific' (gap), but ref-014 already shows universal transferability of automatically generated suffixes across multiple models, contradicting the claim of non-transferability. Additionally, the hypothesis's 'evaluation' section mentions 'datasets of harmful queries from red-teaming studies' but ref-004 and ref-006 do not provide or reference any such shared dataset, making this claim unsupported.

The 'evaluation' section lacks details on the 'harmful content generation rate' metric (e.g., human vs. automated evaluation, specific criteria for 'harmful' content). The 'evaluation' does not name a specific baseline for 'single-model attacks' to isolate the effect of cross-model training.

refined.title: Cross-Model Adversarial Suffix Training for Universal Jailbreak Transferability
refined.summary: We hypothesize that adversarial suffixes trained on a multi-model ensemble improve transferability to unseen models compared to single-model training. We propose a gradient-based optimization framework using a diverse set of harmful prompts and models, evaluated on black-box targets like ChatGPT and Claude.
refined.gap: While ref-014 shows gradient-based suffixes trained on Vicuna transfer to black-box models, it does not compare multi-model vs. single-model training. The gap is whether ensemble training improves transferability beyond single-model methods.
refined.approach: Train adversarial suffixes on a multi-model ensemble (Vicuna-7B, Vicuna-13B, LLaMA-2-7B) using greedy and gradient-based search on 1,000 harmful prompts from red-teaming datasets. The objective is to maximize affirmative responses across models. The core difference from ref-014 is ensemble training with equal weighting, while ref-014 uses single-model training.
refined.evaluation: Measure success rates (binary refusal bypass) on untrained models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) using 500 held-out harmful queries. Compare against baselines: (1) ref-014's Vicuna-trained suffixes, (2) single-model suffixes trained on each ensemble member. Ablation isolates multi-model training effect by testing suffixes trained on individual vs. ensemble models.

hypothesis.title: Constitutional Classifiers for Copyright-Compliant Generation
hypothesis.summary: We propose adapting constitutional classifiers to prevent verbatim reproduction of copyrighted training data. By training classifiers to detect and suppress extractable sequences during generation, we aim to balance utility with legal compliance. The approach uses probabilistic extraction metrics to identify high-risk outputs, which are then filtered or regenerated. Evaluation measures both copyright violation reduction and task performance degradation.
hypothesis.gap: Current alignment techniques focus on safety/harm reduction but neglect copyright concerns from memorized content (ref-004, ref-035).
hypothesis.approach: Integrate probabilistic extraction detection into constitutional classifiers, training them to reject outputs matching training data patterns while preserving functional correctness.
hypothesis.evaluation: Measure extraction success rates post-filtering against baselines (no filtering, random suppression). Assess task performance on code generation (HumanEval) and summarization to quantify utility tradeoffs.

refined.title: Probabilistic Extraction Suppression in Aligned Language Models
refined.summary: We propose integrating probabilistic extraction detection into aligned language models to reduce verbatim reproduction of training data. The method uses a classifier trained to identify high-probability matches to training data during generation, filtering or regenerating outputs that exceed a threshold. This approach targets memorized content while preserving task performance, addressing a gap in current alignment techniques that overlook copyright risks from extractable data.
refined.gap: Current alignment methods (ref-004) focus on safety and harm reduction but do not address verbatim reproduction of training data (ref-035, ref-044). While ref-004 trains classifiers to block harmful content, it does not consider extractable memorized text as a risk. Ref-035 and ref-044 show that models can memorize and reproduce training data, but no work integrates this risk into alignment frameworks.
refined.approach: We train a classifier to detect outputs with high probabilistic extraction scores (ref-029) -- the probability of generating a target sequence given a prompt. During generation, if the classifier identifies a high-risk output (p > τ), the model regenerates the response. The classifier is trained on pairs of (prompt, target) where target is a training data sequence, using a threshold τ determined by validation. The core difference from ref-004 is the addition of extraction risk as a rejection criterion, while retaining its safety filters.
refined.evaluation: We evaluate on code generation (HumanEval, ref-001) and book passage extraction (ref-044). Baselines include: (1) the original constitutional classifier (ref-004) and (2) a model with no filtering. We measure: (a) exact string matches to training data (copyright risk) and (b) task performance (e.g., pass@k for code). An ablation removes the extraction classifier, retaining only safety filters, to isolate the proposed change.

hypothesis.title: Deduplication-Augmented Instruction Tuning for Memorization Reduction

It applies deduplication tools to training data before instruction tuning, hypothesizing that removing duplicates reduces overfitting to specific texts. Evaluation compares memorization rates and task accuracy against models trained on raw data.

hypothesis.title: Jailbreak Transferability Across Aligned Code Models via Many-Shot Prompting
hypothesis.summary: We investigate whether many-shot jailbreak attacks (using hundreds of harmful code examples) can transfer across aligned code models like Codex and LLaMA-2-Chat. The hypothesis is that long-context windows enable cross-model transfer of adversarial prompts. We test this by training attack suffixes on one model and applying them to others, measuring success rates in generating malicious code. The work explores the security implications of shared training data and alignment techniques.
hypothesis.gap: Prior jailbreak research focuses on single-model attacks. The transferability of many-shot attacks across code models, especially those with shared training data, remains unexplored despite the growing use of aligned code assistants in security-critical contexts.
hypothesis.approach: We generate many-shot adversarial prompts by concatenating hundreds of harmful code examples, then apply them to target models. The attack uses gradient-based optimization to find universal suffixes that maximize harmful output probability. We test transferability between Codex, LLaMA-2-Chat, and open-source code models.
hypothesis.evaluation: We measure attack success rates (ASR) on tasks like generating exploit code, comparing same-model vs. cross-model performance. Baselines include single-shot and few-shot attacks. Metrics include ASR, model refusal rates, and output toxicity scores. We also analyze the role of context window size in enabling transferability.

hypothesis.title: Memorization Thresholds in Long-Tailed Data Distributions for Language Models
hypothesis.summary: We propose that language models memorize training data when its frequency falls below a threshold determined by model scale and data distribution. We formalize this as a power-law relationship between memorization probability, data frequency, and model parameters, validated on controlled datasets with varying frequency distributions.
hypothesis.gap: While memorization is linked to data repetition, no formal model exists to predict when it occurs based on data frequency and model scale. Current studies focus on binary memorization without quantifying frequency dependencies.
hypothesis.approach: Create synthetic datasets with controlled long-tailed frequency distributions. Train models of varying sizes and measure memorization rates for different frequency bins. Fit a power-law model to the data to derive the threshold equation.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare predicted vs. observed memorization rates using probabilistic extraction (ref-029) on synthetic and real datasets. Use baselines like GPT-2 and Pythia, with metrics including AUC-ROC for threshold accuracy and correlation between predicted/actual memorization.

This directly contradicts the gap claim about the absence of formal models.

Specifically, there is no mention of testing a null model (e.g., a constant memorization rate across frequencies) or alternative frequency-dependent models (e.g., exponential decay) to verify that the power-law relationship is uniquely supported by the data. Additionally, the 'controlled datasets with varying frequency distributions' are not described in terms of their specific construction (e.g., power-law exponent, vocabulary size, sequence length), making replication impossible.

refined.title: Power-Law Thresholds for Memorization in Long-Tailed Data Distributions
refined.summary: We propose that language models memorize training data when its frequency falls below a power-law threshold determined by model scale and data distribution. We formalize this as a relationship between memorization probability, data frequency, and model parameters, validated on controlled datasets with varying frequency distributions.
refined.gap: While ref-039 models memorization in long-tailed distributions, it does not provide a formal threshold equation to predict memorization based on data frequency and model scale. Ref-048 quantifies memorization growth with data duplication but does not derive a general threshold model. The gap is a lack of a precise, implementable formula to predict memorization risk as a function of frequency and model size.
refined.approach: We create synthetic datasets with controlled long-tailed frequency distributions (power-law exponents α ∈ [1.5, 3.0], vocabulary size 10,000, sequence length 128). We train models of varying sizes (10M-1B parameters) and measure memorization rates for different frequency bins using probabilistic extraction (ref-029). We fit a power-law model: p_memo(f) = k * f^(-β) * m^γ, where f is frequency, m is model size, and k, β, γ are learned parameters. The core difference from ref-039 is the explicit threshold equation derived from empirical data, not just theoretical analysis.
refined.evaluation: We compare predicted vs. observed memorization rates on synthetic and real datasets (C4, ref-011). Baselines include a null model (constant memorization rate) and ref-039's theoretical model. Metrics are AUC-ROC for threshold accuracy and correlation between predicted/actual memorization. Ablation studies isolate model scale (varying m with fixed f) and data distribution (varying α with fixed m). The evaluation tests the central claim that a power-law threshold model outperforms existing approaches in predicting memorization.
